Alright, let's get into it. Thursday, October 29, 2026. Grab a coffee, here's what's hitting the wires.

***

**Money Talk**

-   **US GDP beats expectations, inflation accelerates.**
    Turns out the American economy is still kinda ripping, with Q3 GDP up a surprising 3.4%. But don't pop the champagne just yet – September inflation, measured by the PCE price index, also sped up to an annual 3.7%. So, growth, but at what cost? Classic Fed dilemma. [S1]

-   **Google's parent company Alphabet takes a half-trillion-dollar hit.**
    Ouch. Alphabet just got body-slammed by Wall Street, losing a staggering $500 billion in market value after net profit plunged 25%. Apparently, revenue rising isn't enough when your core Search business is no longer more than half your income. The search for profits continues, apparently. [S11][S37]

-   **Poundland teeters on the brink of collapse.**
    The budget retail chain is filing for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Seems even the lure of cheap essentials can't save everyone from the current economic headwinds. Union's pleading to save it, but the owners rejected a rescue bid. Grim. [S8][S14]

-   **Eli Lilly's obesity drug train keeps on rolling.**
    Wall Street's raising price targets on Lilly because Mounjaro and Zepbound are printing money. The appetite for shedding pounds (and making investors fat) shows no sign of slowing down. Bet the diet soda companies are sweating. [S3]

-   **ECB chief Lagarde steps down early for "freedom of speech."**
    Christine Lagarde is ditching her top central banker gig nine months ahead of schedule, apparently to "speak her mind about world affairs." Sounds like someone's tired of talking in coded central bank language and wants to drop some hot takes. Who can blame her? [S13]

**World Lore**

-   **US and Japan beef up missile production in Asia.**
    The allies are setting up a joint missile production facility in Japan, clearly signaling their "concern" (read: alarm) over China's increasing swagger in the region. Geopolitics, meet the arms race, again. [S21]

-   **China elevates military general, doubles down on party discipline.**
    Ahead of Xi Jinping's expected fourth term, China's Communist Party is elevating a military general to the Politburo and tightening the screws on internal discipline. It's all about loyalty as global tensions simmer and their economy cools. Succession questions remain, but don't hold your breath for answers. [S22][S33]

-   **Israel's election descends into fraud claims and deadlock.**
    Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition lost seats, and now he's trying to delegitimize the results, claiming mass fraud in Arab communities and foreign involvement. Authorities are refuting the claims, but it looks like Israel's political deadlock is, well, deadlocked. Again. [S16][S24][S31]

-   **AI drones are rewriting the rules of the Ukraine war.**
    Artificial intelligence is making these battlefield eyes and ears faster and smarter, with both Russia and Ukraine deploying AI-powered drones. Zelenskyy is even warning that AI could be calling shots on the battlefield as early as next year. Skynet, meet the Donbas. [S25]

-   **Flávio Bolsonaro becomes a Florida Man.**
    Just like his old man, Brazil's far-right senator has packed his bags for Florida after his presidential election loss. Guess the Sunshine State is the official retirement home for international populist losers now. [S30]

**Tech Tea**

-   **Google Search is now less than half of Alphabet's revenue.**
    For the first time ever, the OG cash cow isn't dominating the balance sheet like it used to. While the market cap tumbled, this milestone signals a huge shift for the $4 trillion giant. Is this the beginning of the end for peak Google Search, or just diversification? [S11][S37]

-   **Former Palantir execs launch "Dream" for AI construction.**
    Remember Palantir? Its alums are now building "Dream," an AI world model for construction that's raised $17M from a16z. It's trained on over 100 million square feet of building data, aiming to do for construction what LLMs did for text. Finally, an AI that can yell at drywall. [S43]

-   **Apple's new MacBook Pro gets a PROLED XDR Display, touchscreen.**
    The new MacBook Pro is rocking an OLED display and touchscreen functionality, but for us image-accuracy nerds, the PROLED XDR Display is the real MVP. Apple finally giving the color pros what they want, before they knew they wanted it. [S46]

-   **Data centers could push US climate pollution way up.**
    Brace yourselves: a new analysis suggests the US power sector could pump out 42% *more* carbon dioxide by 2030 than in 2025, thanks to all the fossil fuel infrastructure needed to power these insatiable data centers. Turns out AI has a huge carbon footprint. [S48]

-   **Mistral claims AI model 'Le Chonk' leapfrogs China.**
    The French AI lab is flexing, saying their latest open-weight model, "Le Chonk," now matches or outperforms top models from China in coding and cybersecurity. Sounds like France is ready to enter the AI heavyweight championship. [S53]

**Creator Szn**

-   **The Times of London is testing "macro payments."**
    For those of us who don't want another subscription, The Times is exploring a way for readers to pay a bit more than a micropayment but less than a full sub. It's like a la carte news for the commitment-phobic. Will it stick? [S56]

-   **2026 Midterms are shaping up to be the "Influencer Election."**
    Political campaigns are going all-in recruiting creators, seeing them as the new battleground for voter trust. Disclosure rules are lagging, naturally, but expect your feed to be flooded with political takes from your favorite micro-influencer. [S57]

-   **Retailers still figuring out how to tie AI goals to exec pay.**
    While tech companies are baking AI metrics into executive compensation, retail is lagging. It's a tricky balance: how do you incentivize innovation without creating a "Skynet by Q4" mandate? The C-suite needs to get with the program, or get replaced by a better algorithm. [S58]

-   **Publishers chasing subscriptions ahead of midterms.**
    With referral traffic drying up, news publishers are desperately trying to convert election-season interest into paying subscribers. It's a race to monetize political engagement, because "clicks" don't pay the bills anymore. [S59]

-   **Apple's Safari crackdown pushing ad tech to server-side.**
    Apple's latest moves against tracking mean ad tech is scrambling towards server-side solutions. The IAB Tech Lab's "Trusted Server Framework" is getting buzz, but doubts remain. The walled garden just got a bit taller. [S60]

**Supply Lines**

-   **UPS targets $15B AI data center logistics market.**
    UPS just had a solid Q3 beat and is raising its 2026 guidance, explicitly shifting towards logistics for the booming AI data center industry. They're eyeing a massive $15 billion opportunity, betting that moving servers is the next big thing. Smart money says they're right. [S76][S77][S79]

-   **Fresno carrier DTL to deploy 75 Kodiak driverless trucks.**
    DTL Transport has inked a binding deal to put Kodiak's autonomous driving tech into 75 of their trucks, starting on the Dallas-El Paso and Dallas-Atlanta routes. This is a big win for Kodiak and a clear sign that self-driving long-haul is no longer just sci-fi. [S61]

-   **FedEx drawing parcel shippers to air freight for high-value cargo.**
    FedEx saw 12% annual revenue growth in Q3 and is strategically pushing its air freight services to traditionally parcel-focused customers, especially those in high-value segments like AI and data centers. They're positioning themselves as the go-to for urgent, valuable tech components. [S66][S87][S89]

-   **Soaring diesel costs squeeze carrier profits.**
    The CEO of the Florida Trucking Association is warning that rising diesel, insurance, and equipment costs are putting "mounting financial pressure" on motor carriers. Fuel prices, exacerbated by Middle East conflict, are always the first to bite, and it's hitting the bottom line hard. [S63]

-   **Cold chain cyberattack exposes logistics vulnerabilities.**
    A recent hack on French supermarket refrigeration systems showed how remote controls can cause real physical losses. This is a massive warning for cold stores, pharma warehouses, and connected reefer fleets: your digital vulnerabilities can lead to very analog (and expensive) spoilage. [S75]

**Speed Round**

-   The UK Chancellor's budget was "micro," surprising exactly zero economists.
-   A new Lego store in Norwich drew hundreds, proving adult disposable income is still strong for nostalgic plastic bricks.
-   Trump accused Democrats of perjury in the Alaska Senate race. Shocking.
-   Cape Canaveral is in a new "boom cycle" of rocket launches, outpacing the Cold War era.
-   Dream, a new startup, just raised $17M to build AI world models for construction.
-   DoorDash just made a $17 billion bet on Instacart to stave off Amazon and Walmart.
-   Withings now requires a subscription to sync your health data; an open-source project is fighting back.
